content.question: How is the climate of India broadly described?
content.note:
India has a Tropical Monsoonal Climate.
The climate is dominated by the reversal of monsoon winds (Southwest and Northeast).
Note: This pattern ensures distinct seasons: a hot summer, a rainy monsoon, and a cool winter.

content.question: Heavy rainfall during the months of October and November is received by which coast?
content.note:
The Coromandel Coast receives heavy rainfall in October and November.
This is caused by the Retreating Monsoon (Northeast Monsoon) picking up moisture from the Bay of Bengal.
Note: While most of India gets rain from the SW Monsoon, this coast stays dry during that time.

content.question: Trees like sal, teak, neem, sheesham, and sandalwood are found in which type of forests?
content.note:
These trees are characteristic of Tropical Deciduous Forests.
These forests are found in regions with rainfall between 70 cm and 200 cm.
Note: They shed their leaves for about 6 to 8 weeks in dry summer to conserve water.

content.question: The temperate grasslands of South America are called what?
content.note:
The Pampas are fertile South American lowlands.
They are primarily located in Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil.
Note: They are ideal for cattle ranching and wheat farming.

content.question: What is the groundwater stored in the spaces between layers of hard rock below the water table called?
content.note:
Aquifers are geological formations of rocks/sand that hold water.
Water moves through these layers under the influence of gravity and pressure. Related info: When water is trapped between two impermeable layers, it forms a Confined Aquifer.

content.question: At what altitude is the geostationary orbit located?
content.note:
A Geostationary Orbit is at an altitude of approximately 35,786 km (commonly rounded to 36,000 km) above the equator.
At this height, the satellite's orbital period matches Earth's rotation, making it appear stationary from the ground. Use: Essential for communication and weather satellites.

content.question: What is the coastal part of the oceanic water bodies that slopes seaward and is structurally part of the continental mainland called?
content.note:
The Continental Shelf is the submerged edge of a continent.
It is relatively shallow (depth up to 200m) and is the most biologically productive part of the ocean.
Note: It provides most of the world's seafood and offshore oil/gas.

content.question: Dhuandhar Falls and Kapildhara Falls are located on which river?
content.note:
The Narmada River creates these spectacular waterfalls.
Dhuandhar (Smoke cascade) is located in Bhedaghat, Jabalpur, where the river falls through marble rocks.
Note: Narmada is a west-flowing river that flows through a rift valley.

content.question: The Himalayas belong to which type of mountain range?
content.note:
The Himalayas are Fold Mountains.
They were formed by the collision of the Indo-Australian Plate and the Eurasian Plate, causing the sedimentary rocks to fold upward.
Note: They are 'Young' because they formed recently in geological time.

content.question: Kolleru Lake, one of the largest freshwater lakes in India, is located in which state?
content.note:
Kolleru Lake is one of the largest freshwater lakes in India, located in Andhra Pradesh.
It sits between the Krishna and Godavari deltas.
Note: It is a designated Ramsar site and an important habitat for migratory birds like the Grey Pelican.

content.question: Which is the highest peak of South India or the Western Ghats?
content.note:
Anamudi is the highest peak in the Western Ghats and all of South India, with an elevation of 2,695 meters.
It is located in the Eravikulam National Park in Kerala. Nickname: It is often called the 'Everest of South India'.

content.question: Which sea existed in place of the Himalayas before the tectonic shift?
content.note:
The Tethys Sea was a prehistoric ocean.
As the Indian plate moved north and collided with Asia, the sediments of the Tethys were squeezed and uplifted to form the Himalayas. Evidence: Marine fossils are still found high up in the Himalayan ranges.

content.question: What is the rhythmic rise and fall of sea water twice a day called?
content.note:
Tides are the rise and fall of sea levels caused by the combined effects of the gravitational forces exerted by the Moon and the Sun.
Most places experience two high tides and two low tides every day.
Note: The moon has a stronger effect because it is closer to Earth.

content.question: All three latitude lines—the Tropic of Cancer, Equator, and the Tropic of Capricorn—pass through which continent?
content.note:
Africa is the only continent through which the Tropic of Cancer, the Equator, and the Tropic of Capricorn all pass.
This is due to its vast latitudinal extent across the middle of the globe.
Note: Most of the continent lies within the Tropics.

content.question: Which layer is the uppermost boundary of our atmosphere, extending from the top of the thermosphere up to 10,000 kilometers?
content.note:
The Exosphere is the outermost layer of the atmosphere.
Here, the air is extremely thin, and atoms and molecules escape into space. Boundary: It starts around 700 km and blends into the vacuum of space at about 10,000 km.

content.question: What is the name given to the path along the Pacific Ocean where active volcanoes are found and frequent earthquakes occur?
content.note:
The Ring of Fire is a major area in the basin of the Pacific Ocean.
It contains about 75% of the world's active volcanoes and 90% of the world's earthquakes occur here. Cause: It is the result of Plate Tectonics (subduction zones).

content.question: India's largest inland saltwater lake, Sambhar, is located in which state?
content.note:
Sambhar Lake is India's largest inland saltwater lake.
It is located in the desert circuit of Rajasthan near Jaipur.
Note: It is a major source of salt production and a key wintering area for flamingos.

content.question: The Shevaroy Hills are located in which state of India?
content.note:
The Shevaroy Hills are a part of the Eastern Ghats located in Tamil Nadu, near the city of Salem.
They are known for their temperate climate and coffee plantations.
Note: The hill station of Yercaud is situated here.

content.question: Which type of forest is most widely spread in India and also known as 'Monsoon Forests'?
content.note:
Tropical Deciduous Forests are the most widespread in India.
They are called Monsoon Forests because they shed their leaves during the dry season.
Note: They are divided into Moist Deciduous and Dry Deciduous based on water availability.

content.question: Zanskar, Hunza, Shyok, Gilgit, and Nubra are tributaries of which river?
content.note:
These are all major Himalayan tributaries of the Indus River.
They join the Indus in the Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan regions.
Note: The Shyok is known as the 'River of Death' due to its difficult terrain.

content.question: The area served by a canal system through water supply for irrigation and other purposes is called what?
content.note:
The Command Area is the area that can be irrigated by a canal system.
It is the specific region that receives water from a particular dam or reservoir project. Management: Command Area Development (CAD) programs focus on maximizing agricultural production in these areas.

content.question: Which drainage pattern is formed when streams flow in different directions from a central peak or dome-like structure?
content.note:
A Radial Drainage Pattern looks like the spokes of a wheel.
It forms when rivers flow outward in all directions from a central dome or volcanic cone. Example: The rivers originating from the Amarkantak Mountain (like Narmada and Son) show this pattern.

content.question: What shows a unidirectional flow in an ecosystem?
content.note:
In an ecosystem, Energy flow is Unidirectional.
It flows from the Sun to Producers (plants) then to Consumers (animals).
Note: Unlike nutrients, which are recycled, energy is lost as heat at each level and cannot go back to the source.

content.question: The strong, gusty, hot, and dry winds that blow in May and June in northern and northwestern India are called what?
content.note:
The Loo is a strong, hot, and dry summer afternoon wind from the west which blows over the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
Exposure to it can cause fatal heatstroke. Season: It is common in May and June.

content.question: Which region of India is now considered an Ecological Hotspot?
content.note:
The Western Ghats are one of the world's eight 'hottest hotspots' of biological diversity.
They have a high degree of endemism (species found nowhere else).
Note: They help regulate the Indian monsoon by intercepting rain-bearing winds.

content.question: Where are Kishtwar National Park and Dachigam Wildlife Sanctuary located?
content.note:
Kishtwar and Dachigam are in Jammu and Kashmir.
Dachigam is famous for being the last home of the Hangul (Kashmir Stag).
Note: Kishtwar is known for its high-altitude landscape and snow leopards.

content.question: Which place/region is the natural habitat of the Indian Wild Ass?
content.note:
The Little Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is the only place in the world where the Indian Wild Ass (Khur) is found.
This saline desert provides the specific vegetation and isolation they need.
Note: It is protected under the Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary.

content.question: Which mountain range is known as the 'Backbone of South America'?
content.note:
The Andes is the longest continental mountain range in the world.
It runs along the entire western coast of South America. Fact: It contains Aconcagua, the highest peak outside of Asia.

content.question: Which soil is rich in lime, iron, alumina, and magnesia, and develops deep cracks during hot weather?
content.note:
Black Soil (also known as Regur) is famous for growing Cotton.
It has a high clay content and excellent water-holding capacity.
Note: When it dries, it develops deep cracks, which helps in self-aeration of the soil.

content.question: Majuli, the world's largest river island, is located in which state?
content.note:
Majuli is a large river island in the Brahmaputra River, Assam.
It was the first island to be made a district in India. Threat: Due to the massive discharge and speed of the Brahmaputra, the island faces severe erosion every year.
